newsitem.title: USA: Massachusetts unveils proposed regulations on tobacco.
newsitem.headline: Massachusetts unveils proposed regulations on tobacco.

text.p: Massachusetts on Tuesday released details of proposed regulations that would force tobacco companies to list all the ingredients of cigarettes on the side of packages sold in the state.

Under the proposed regulations, tobacco companies will have to file an annual report with the Department of Public Health that lists all additives for each brand sold in the state. In keeping with federal procedures for food additives, the measure requires that tobacco ingredients be listed in descending order according to weight and quantity.
The proposed regulations would also require cigarette packages to include a nicotine rating system, reporting how much of the drug is delivered for average and for heavy smokers.

The Mass. Department of Public Health said that with the introduction of light and ultralight cigarettes, consumers' have changed their smoking habits by smoking more cigarettes or inhaling more deeply.
Cigarettes, snuff and chewing tobacco are affected by the proposed regulations.
In August, Massachusetts became the first state in the country to pass a law requiring cigarette packages to list all ingredients. The law is scheduled to go into effect on July 1.

Tobacco companies have argued that listing their ingredients would divulge trade secrets. The companies said in court documents they would consider not selling ciarettes in the state if the law is enacted.

Four major tobacco companies, Philip Morris Cos Inc, R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp, Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp, a unit of B.A.T Industries Plc and Lorillard Tobacco Co, a unit of Loews Corp, have filed a lawsuit against the state contesting the law. Hearings are scheduled to begin December 3.

The state will begin public hearings on the proposed regulations beginning in late December or early January and is expected to finalize the regulations by early spring, Connolly said.
"We'll be submitting detailed comments on these (regulations) at the appropriate time," said David Remes, a lawyer representing the four tobacco companies.
